label: Cardiogenic shock
summary: A low cardiac output state from heart dysfunction that causes tissue hypoperfusion, most often after acute MI. The SCAI scale stages it from A (at risk) to E (extremis) so teams can escalate early.

levers.why: Loss of working LV muscle, most often from MI, lowers stroke volume.
Hypotension lowers coronary perfusion pressure, which worsens ischemia in a downward spiral.

nursingPriorities: Trend MAP, lactate, urine output, mental status and skin perfusion together; one normal value does not prove adequate perfusion.
Escalate early: SCAI stage B (hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion) is the window before lactate rises.
After MI with shock, prepare for emergency transfer to the cath lab.

relations.why: LV pump failure, most often from acute MI, is the commonest cause.
Poor tissue perfusion shifts cells to anaerobic metabolism.
Tissues extract more oxygen when delivery falls.
Vasoconstriction diverts blood from the skin to vital organs.
Kidney perfusion drops with low cardiac output.
Measured low output with high filling pressure defines the syndrome hemodynamically.
A vasopressor restores perfusion pressure when MAP is low.
An inotrope raises contractility and cardiac output.
An inodilator raises contractility while lowering afterload.
Emergency revascularization of the culprit artery after MI improves survival.
Counterpulsation can support selected patients, though routine use in MI shock did not lower mortality.
A microaxial pump unloads the LV and adds forward flow.
Full circulatory and respiratory support for refractory shock.
